## 5. Specs as the input of coding agents, and safety

This section answers the third question: whether the specifications are the best input for the agents that write the code, so that the code is correct and safe. It starts from what agents did with real tasks, then takes the three classes of finding that decide whether an implementation is safe.

| Class | Section | High | Medium | Low | Total |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| No stated proof, authorization or bound | [5.2](#52-effects-without-a-stated-proof-authorization-or-bound) | 9 | 34 | 17 | 60 |
| Failure behavior not stated | [5.3](#53-failure-unknown-outcomes-and-continuation) | 5 | 28 | 13 | 46 |
| No check holds the table or the rule | [5.4](#54-tables-and-rules-that-no-check-holds) | 0 | 24 | 48 | 72 |
| **All** | | **14** | **86** | **78** | **178** |

### 5.1 What the dry runs show

The twelve dry runs confirm the other sections from the side of the reader. An agent given a real task finds most of the rules it needs. It still guesses five to nine times, six at the median, and it ends at a median confidence of 3 of 5 ([section 2.3](#23-what-a-coding-agent-loads-and-where-it-guesses)). About six guesses in ten come from routing, form or missing general rules that text work can repair. The rest are choices that only the owner can make.

The dry-run lanes filed 74 candidates, and verification refuted 22 of them. The material holds 50 verified findings: 1 High, 15 Medium and 34 Low. The areas with the most are API (10), CLI (6), CTX (6), MOS (5), GOV (4) and CEPH (4). REC, OCP and MIL hold 3 each, SUB and ARC 2 each, and ADD and HAR 1 each.

The drafter of this section sorted every guess the agents reported into one class, and nobody verified the sorting: (a) routing or code location, (b) a general rule that the specs lack, (c) a choice about the new feature that only the owner can make, (d) a contradiction, a stale statement or an unclear sentence.

| Task | Bytes loaded | Guesses | (a) | (b) | (c) | (d) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| T1 NIC description | 54,122 | 6 | 1 | 4 | 0 | 1 |
| T2 KubeVirt destroy stop | 78,600 | 6 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 |
| T3 install continuation | 114,183 | 5 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 3 |
| T4 `machine exec --timeout` | 73,951 | 6 | 0 | 2 | 4 | 0 |
| T5 new service kind | 155,000 | 9 | 0 | 3 | 4 | 2 |
| T6 Ceph unreachable host | 84,907 | 6 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 3 |
| T7 new add-on package | 88,000 | 9 | 4 | 2 | 3 | 0 |
| T8 `secret show` renewal | 62,000 | 6 | 0 | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| T9 NVMe secure erase | 84,152 | 9 | 0 | 2 | 6 | 1 |
| T10 grant expiry | 65,100 | 9 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 0 |
| T11 controller package | 66,330 | 6 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 1 |
| T12 ambiguous root disk | 52,055 | 5 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 3 |
| Total | 978,400 | 82 | 12 | 23 | 31 | 16 |

The findings that matter most:

- [CLI-3](#cli-3): `--keep-going` continues after a failed removal only when the stop "explicitly" confines the failure (`specs/cli/stops.md:20`). No spec names which stops carry that attestation. In code three stops set it, and no test holds the field. An agent adding a stop cannot know whether to set it.
- [HAR-5](#har-5), [GOV-3](#gov-3) and [GOV-4](#gov-4): the index does not route to the sections that own destructive proof and authorization (`specs/index.md:41`), to interrupted-install recovery (`specs/index.md:40`), or to `machine exec` sessions (`specs/index.md:43`). The agents for T2, T3, T4 and T9 loaded whole pages or missed the owner section.
- [CEPH-68](#ceph-68), [CEPH-70](#ceph-70) and [REC-36](#rec-36): the Ceph removal text says a surviving host "keeps the refusal below" but names no refusal (`specs/ceph.md:2480`). It names tiebreaker refusals that the stop catalog holds as reasons of one stop. Its restatement in state reconciliation drops the bare-metal path. Half of the T6 guesses come from these three.
- [SUB-17](#sub-17): a hosted KubeVirt Machine "refuses new lifecycle work before registration" (`specs/substrates.md:1626`), stated as a target rule. The same section describes a working hosted lifecycle. The refusal is an interim state and should be a `Not yet met` line for B1622.
- [CLI-22](#cli-22): `specs/cli.md:1233` says the `machine info` result has the same fields as the listing. `specs/cli/output.md:581` and the code say it extends them. The copy drifted from its owner.
- [CTX-21](#ctx-21) and [REC-17](#rec-17): the host-package table (`specs/controller.md:247`) names no code symbol and no test. The reference-edge catalog lists managed-service requirements for only some kinds (`specs/state-reconciliation.md:1061`). An agent that trusts either table builds less than the code does.
- [ARC-17](#arc-17): the selection-section template in `specs/architecture.md:1309` has five parts. The skill and the pages use three. An agent adding a kind cannot follow both.
- [OCP-8](#ocp-8) and [API-46](#api-46): an ambiguous root-disk inventory "refuses before insertion" with no stop code (`specs/openshift-clusters.md:56`). The session policy input grammar lives only in code (`specs/api/session-access-policy.md:50`).

Why it happens: the findings show three causes. The index routes to pages and to a few sections, not to the owner of a destructive or recovery rule, so the agents read up to 155,000 bytes. Rules are restated on several pages, and the copies drift (CLI-22, REC-36, CEPH-70). The corpus states each feature's rules but rarely the general rule for adding a new field, stop, kind or package. The agents then copy the nearest precedent, as T1, T5, T8 and T9 did.

What is right and should stay: T11 reached confidence 4, because one section owns the host-package split and the install and uninstall rules. In T10 and T12 the agents also found the fail-closed rules and the apply-time proof where the specs place them.

What fixes the class: routing and form work removes the 12 routing guesses and the 16 text defects. General rules on how a new field, stop, kind or package is added, each with a test that holds it, remove the 23 guesses of class (b). The 31 owner choices of class (c) remain. A brief can list them as questions before implementation, but the specs should not hold them in advance. [Section 7](#7-the-plan) gives the plan.

### 5.2 Effects without a stated proof, authorization or bound

Most effect rules in the corpus state their proof and their failure behavior, but a set of rules on secret, access and erase paths does not. In three High findings and one Medium finding, the code already does what the weak text permits, so the gap is a live defect, not only a reading risk. The text does not catch this because few effect rules name the test that holds them.

The class holds 60 findings: 9 High, 34 Medium and 17 Low. 55 are single defects and 5 are patterns of form. 45 are new, 4 were reported by audit 004 and are still present, 4 are tracked by an open item, 2 are settled and 5 Low findings were not judged. Nine were found by more than one lane.

| Area | High | Medium | Low | Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| API | 3 | 4 | 1 | 8 |
| CLI | 1 | 6 | 1 | 8 |
| SUB | 1 | 5 | 1 | 7 |
| CTX | 0 | 4 | 2 | 6 |
| CEPH | 0 | 3 | 3 | 6 |
| SEC | 3 | 1 | 0 | 4 |

The other seven areas hold 21 findings, among them one High in OCP.

**The code already follows the unsafe rule.**

- [API-3](#api-3): the erase precondition "verified BMC TLS" tests only `bmc.tls.verification`, while the BMC address may be `http://` (`specs/api/machines.md:1060-1061`). The erase code uses the same field-only test, while other consumers require `https`. So a disk erase can run over a plain HTTP BMC.
- [SEC-1](#sec-1): an elevated `secret set` refuses when sudo logs input (`specs/secrets.md:96-102`), but no page covers sudo's output log. The raw reveals (`secret show`, `cluster kubeconfig`, `cluster keyring`) write secrets to standard output under sudo. The privilege test passes a listing that sets only `log_output`.
- [SEC-2](#sec-2): the hold on effect material refuses `generate --renew` and `set`, but not `secret delete` (`specs/secrets.md:153`). The code does not check holds on delete either, so delete then generate replaces the only copy that any command can reveal.
- [MOS-21](#mos-21): the text says unregister removes "only a consumer this installation's record names, owned or `pending`" (`specs/managed-os.md:1194-1196`). A pending record names no consumer, and the worker adopts any certificate it finds, then unregisters it on destroy.

**The proof exists only in code, or is never linked.** [API-2](#api-2): destroy deletes a host account and archives its home, but the ownership mark, the home path and the sudoers content check are not in the spec (`specs/api/machines.md:758`). An agent that works from the text alone can delete an operator's account with the same name. [CLI-1](#cli-1): two password prompts require "proof that sudo will not record" input (`specs/cli.md:1381`) and do not link the one place that defines it.

**Two trust rules disagree.** [OCP-1](#ocp-1): the private publication contract forbids a fetch that disables verification (`specs/infrastructure-services.md:577-578`), while D269 admits `disableVerification` for private boot media, so two agents build opposite behavior. [SEC-4](#sec-4): the security page still calls authored add-ons inert data that grant no privilege (`specs/security.md:1048`), while authored OLM add-ons now run an operator with the privileges their CSV requests.

**No boundary at all.** [SUB-1](#sub-1): each libvirt guest gets a VNC display on loopback (`specs/substrates.md:947`), and no page states who may open it.

Below these, four patterns ([CTX-P12](#ctx-p12), [MOS-P14](#mos-p14), [SVC-P4](#svc-p4), [API-P4](#api-p4)) write "bounded" on a safety path with no value and no Go constant, for example `specs/controller.md:341-342`.

The findings show three causes. First, a proof is defined once in code and only named in the text, so a second implementation has nothing to follow ([API-2](#api-2), [CLI-1](#cli-1)). Second, a proof term is restated on several pages and the copies drift: "verified BMC" has three meanings in [API-3](#api-3), and [OCP-1](#ocp-1) was never reconciled with a later decision. Third, a test rarely holds the rule. Of 1,672 effect rules, 72% state their proof and 74% their failure, but only 11% name a test ([section 2.9](#29-effect-rules-proof-failure-and-test)). That is why the code in [SEC-1](#sec-1) passes its own test while the gap stays.

Two things are right and should stay. The cross-lane table of 16 destructive steps shows that power-off, secret deletion, encryption rotation and virtual Machine removal each state their ownership proof, authorization, unknown outcome and crash behavior, and the pages agree. And of about 40 secret-referencing API fields checked, none lacks a material class.

The fix is to give each proof term one anchored definition (verified BMC, the sudo I/O-log proof, owned and pending registration, the managed-login mark) and to link it from every consumer instead of restating it. Each effect rule on a destructive, secret or privilege path then names its test, and each bound names its Go constant. The code changes that [API-3](#api-3), [SEC-1](#sec-1), [SEC-2](#sec-2) and [MOS-21](#mos-21) need belong in tracked items, not in spec edits. [Section 7](#7-the-plan) owns the details.

### 5.3 Failure, unknown outcomes and continuation

The engine in `specs/state-reconciliation.md` has a clear model of failure: an attempt ends `done`, `failed` or `unknown`, and a continuation resolves every unproved block before it retries. The domain pages do not always use that model. Some stop catalog rows and some domain remedies give a different answer than the engine. Many guards say what they check but not what happens when the check fails. The defects sit on destroy, recovery and access paths, so this class holds five High findings.

The audit found 46 findings in this class: 5 High, 28 Medium and 13 Low. Of them, 45 are single defects and 1 is a pattern of form. By status, 33 are new, 5 were reported by audit 004 and are still present, 2 are tracked by an open item, and 6 are Low findings whose status nobody judged. Four were found by more than one lane.

| Area | High | Medium | Low | Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| CEPH | 0 | 5 | 3 | 8 |
| CLI | 0 | 3 | 4 | 7 |
| MOS | 2 | 3 | 2 | 7 |
| REC | 1 | 1 | 3 | 5 |
| OCP | 0 | 5 | 0 | 5 |
| CTX | 0 | 4 | 0 | 4 |
| SEC | 1 | 2 | 1 | 4 |
| API, SUB, SVC, ADD and MIL together | 1 | 5 | 0 | 6 |

The High findings are REC-1, SEC-51, MOS-1, MOS-2 and ADD-2.

**Domain rules that disagree with the engine.** In [REC-1](#rec-1), six "adapter gave no usable outcome" stops have certainty `possible`, for example `install.no-outcome` at `specs/cli/stops.md:449`. The catalog header says every certainty except `unproved` records the attempt `failed`. The engine maps an `unknown` adapter outcome to an `unknown` block, which is what the code records, and sibling stops such as `addon.outcome-unknown` are `unproved`. Two rules give two answers for the same firing. In [ADD-2](#add-2), `specs/add-ons.md:467` gives a failed read the same remedy as a foreign object: "destroy and apply again". The engine's rule is to continue the operation, which observes the block again (`specs/state-reconciliation.md:589`). An operator who meets one transient API error is told to destroy a whole cluster. [CEPH-48](#ceph-48) shows the same gap on the Ceph pages. They state no per-effect proof of completion, no effect or partial realization, and "absence does not permit repeating bootstrap or a setter" (`specs/ceph.md:2169`) leaves an unknown with no stated exit.

**Effects that removal or rebind does not see.** In [MOS-1](#mos-1), removal is `skip` for an installation whose records hold no marker preparation (`specs/managed-os.md:1206`). Under a subscription package source, the installer registers before any such preparation exists. A destroy in that window leaves an orphan consumer on the Satellite, and no page says so. In [SEC-51](#sec-51), the Ceph registry login can be rebound by a continuation, but no page says whether each host's retained `podman-auth.json` is rewritten (`specs/secrets.md:563-565`).

**Guards with no failure outcome.** In [MOS-2](#mos-2), the SSH source filter checks the peer, refuses socket activation and verifies the policy again (`specs/managed-os.md:2384-2385`). The spec does not tie these checks to `ssh-admission`, and it does not say what stays in place after a failed verification. A wrong implementation of this rule can lock operators out of a host. In [OCP-14](#ocp-14), the kept kubeconfig is handed over only when it is a regular file within 64 KiB (`specs/openshift-clusters.md:655-657`). For any other file the code skips the copy, and the inverse then deletes the only admin credential, against D124. In [REC-11](#rec-11), the one retry of an inconclusive removal "performs nothing otherwise" (`specs/state-reconciliation.md:699`), but the spec does not say what that attempt records.

**Remedies that do not work.** In [CTX-24](#ctx-24), the remedy for an added package set over 1024 packages is `uninstall --keep-packages` (`specs/controller.md:333-336`). Uninstall refuses on any host that holds a context, so the only path left destroys every environment.

**Why it happens.** Each domain page writes its failure text next to its effect instead of linking the engine's outcome and resolution rules. The copies drift: the stop rows in REC-1 and the add-on remedy in ADD-2 each follow their own reading, and the code follows the copy (`internal/addons/instance/unresolved.go`). Guards are written as the success condition and end at "refuses" or "skips", with no code, no state and no continuation. The code then decides on its own, as the silent skip in OCP-14 and the `unknown` record in REC-11 show. The baseline gives the scale: 74% of effect rules state their failure behavior, and only 11% name a test that holds it ([section 2.9](#29-effect-rules-proof-failure-and-test)).

**What is right and should stay.** The engine's attempt-outcome and resolution tables in `specs/state-reconciliation.md` give one mapping from outcome to block state, and every finding above can be resolved by linking them. The managed OS, substrate, OpenShift and infrastructure service pages already state, per effect family, what proves completion, no effect, partial realization and unknown.

**What fixes the class.** Each domain page links the engine for the outcome and the continuation, and keeps only its own proofs. Each guard names its stop code, the state it leaves and the command that continues. A remedy for a condition that may be transient is the command that observes again, never a destroy. [Section 7](#7-the-plan) owns the order and the details.

### 5.4 Tables and rules that no check holds

The corpus says the code owns every inventory: a spec points at the code, or a named test holds the table equal to it (C6), and a required behavior names its test (C13). The audit found that this rule holds for some tables, but many lists are still copied by hand with no test, and several tests that look like they hold a table compare only part of it. Where a test exists, the text often does not name it. So an agent cannot tell a checked table from one that may have drifted.

The class holds 72 findings: 24 Medium and 48 Low, none High. 59 are single defects and 13 are patterns of form. 43 are new, 11 were reported by audit 004 and are still present, 1 is tracked by an open item, and 17 Low findings were not judged for status. Nine were found by more than one lane.

| Area | Medium | Low | Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| CLI | 3 | 7 | 10 |
| API | 2 | 7 | 9 |
| CEPH | 3 | 5 | 8 |
| MOS | 1 | 5 | 6 |
| REC | 3 | 2 | 5 |
| CTX | 1 | 4 | 5 |
| SUB | 1 | 4 | 5 |
| MIL | 0 | 5 | 5 |
| Other eight areas | 10 | 9 | 19 |

The baseline gives the scale. Of 71 inventories that enumerate what the code also enumerates, 34 are held by no test, and 6 of the 23 unheld ones that were compared with the code had drifted ([section 2.8](#28-inventories-and-the-tests-that-hold-them)). Only 11% of effect rules name the test that holds them ([section 2.9](#29-effect-rules-proof-failure-and-test)).

The defects that matter most:

- **A secrecy rule with no paths and no test.** [MOS-80](#mos-80): `specs/managed-os.md:332-339` says the `%post` "removes every retained copy of the Kickstart". It names neither the three files the code removes nor the test that holds the step. Two secrecy sentences depend on it. An agent that rebuilds the `%post` from the spec can drop the step and leave an activation key or a disk passphrase on the installed disk.
- **A test name that does not exist.** [SEC-32](#sec-32): the Required security proof table cites `test_the_read_after_a_stall_runs_under_no_log_and_never_fails_the_wait_itself` (`specs/security.md:1115`). No such test exists. The Go names in the table are checked, but the collection's Python names are not, so nothing caught the rename.
- **Held tables that are only partly held.** [CEPH-45](#ceph-45): the six refusal-table tests parse the Path column and drop it, and the Ceph test never exercises `CephPlacementPolicy` (`specs/ceph.md:594-598`). [HAR-19](#har-19): `TestCommandCatalogMatchesSpec` compares paths, flag names, shorthands and closed values, but not defaults, required markers or results (`internal/cli/docs_commands_test.go:256-259`). [ARC-19](#arc-19): `make docs-check` runs only the tests that `docs-checks.txt` lists, and about 11 tests that hold spec tables are not on it (`specs/architecture.md:1434-1436`).
- **Hand-copied lists that drifted.** [CLI-35](#cli-35): the list of context-free commands leaves out `explain`, which the code marks context-free (`specs/cli/commands.md:11`). The test that is said to hold "these lists" does not read the prose. [GOV-9](#gov-9): the list of admitted operator utilities omits `machine cp`, `media eject`, `cluster update-admin-creds` and others (`specs/project.md:187-190`). [ARC-7](#arc-7): the package table disagrees with `packageRoles`, and its test checks one row (`specs/architecture.md:325`).
- **Two owners for one list.** [SEC-17](#sec-17): `specs/security.md:219-222` defines the run-nothing set by the catalog link, and `specs/cli/output.md` keeps its own hand-written list of the same commands.
- **Refusals with no code.** [HAR-16](#har-16): in a sample of 33 refusal sentences, about 26 name neither a stop code nor a refusal-table row (`specs/substrates.md:786-787`). [CEPH-P3](#ceph-p3): about 42 Ceph refusal names live only in prose (`specs/ceph.md:1576`), although `adapterRefusals` in the code pairs each with its code. [OCP-6](#ocp-6): Selection says the refusal table states every refusal, but several refusals have no row (`specs/openshift-clusters.md:36`).

Why it happens: C6 states the target, but nothing enforces it on new text. A page can add a list, or a test name, without any gate failing. `TestDocsChecksListIsComplete` finds holding tests by name prefix and suffix, so a test outside that naming is silently left out of `make docs-check` ([ARC-19](#arc-19)). The text also says "held" for a table whose test drops a column ([CEPH-45](#ceph-45)) or does not read the prose at all ([CLI-35](#cli-35)), so the claim of a check is itself unchecked. The 11 findings from audit 004 that are still present show that a reported drift is fixed in one place while the copy stays.

What should stay: where a test generates or compares the whole table, the table agrees with the code. Examples are the command result fields in `specs/cli/output.md`, the Ceph listener table and the native service family table. Of the 23 unheld inventories compared with the code, 17 still agree, so most copies are correct today: the gap is that nothing keeps them so.

What fixes the class: each inventory either becomes a link to the code that owns it or gets a test that compares every column, listed where `make docs-check` runs it. A rule that says "held" names the test, and the cited test names, Python included, are checked to exist. Refusal sentences name their stop code or their table row. [Section 7](#7-the-plan) owns the steps.

## 6. Delivery pages

The milestone pages, the backlog, the decision log and the delivered record are half of the corpus by size. They are the owner's working records and not specifications, and the audit judged them for the use an agent makes of them.

| Class | Section | High | Medium | Low | Total |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Delivery state and record shape | [6.1](#61-milestone-pages-and-delivered-records) | 0 | 37 | 67 | 104 |
| The decision log | [6.2](#62-the-decision-log) | 0 | 16 | 19 | 35 |
| **All** | | **0** | **53** | **86** | **139** |

### 6.1 Milestone pages and delivered records

The milestone pages work as an index by id, but often not as a brief for one item. An agent that opens an item finds delivery narrative, test lists and stale state around the few lines it needs. Sometimes the state is wrong: an item reads as ready when it is not, or an id leads to a record about other work. The audit found the reverse leak too: normative pages carry delivery state that belongs on milestone pages.

The class holds 104 findings: 37 Medium and 67 Low, with no Blocking and no High. 98 are single defects and 6 are patterns of form. 62 are new and 32 were reported by audit 004 and are still present. Six Low findings were not judged for status, 3 are tracked by an open item and 1 is settled. 14 were found by more than one lane. Most sit on the milestone pages themselves. The rest are delivery state written inside normative pages, where they count under the page's own area:

| Area | Medium | Low | Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| MIL | 16 | 57 | 73 |
| OCP | 4 | 2 | 6 |
| ADD | 2 | 3 | 5 |
| SEC | 4 | 0 | 4 |
| REC | 3 | 0 | 3 |
| SUB | 3 | 0 | 3 |
| Other seven areas | 5 | 5 | 10 |

The scale is in [section 2.11](#211-delivery-pages): 259 of 365 open items (71%) await the owner's acceptance, and `delivered.md` holds 474 records at 1,116,589 bytes.

**State that an agent cannot act on.** [MIL-5](#mil-5) (`specs/milestones.md:47-51`): the rules never define "open items". So by the letter of the In-sequence rule, M1 stays first while its queue of 144 items waits for acceptance, and about 70% of the item rows are rows an agent can only skip. [MIL-3](#mil-3) (`specs/milestones.md:26-28`): four M1 items are `in progress` with no slice. They appear in no Active slices row, and the docs check exempts them, so an agent asked for active work does not see this program. [MIL-41](#mil-41) (`specs/milestones/m1.md:2993-2994`): seven items await operator acceptance but name no operator gate, and four of them name no exit evidence at all.

**An item that reads as ready but is not.** [MIL-50](#mil-50) (`specs/milestones/m2.md:3247-3248`): eight sections end with "D261 authorizes implementation". This breaks the scope rule that no decision authorizes implementation, and seven of the eight items are `Needs definition`. [MIL-53](#mil-53) (`specs/milestones/m3.md:1167-1172`): B719 is `Specified` and in progress, but its own text says the remainder has no typed source, so an agent must invent a public API to finish it.

**Ids that lead to the wrong work.** [MIL-23](#mil-23) (`specs/milestones/backlog.md:9302-9303`): X461/B1393 and X462/B1394 name one delivery in the m1 rows and another in the decisions and the delivered records. Two safety items then have no delivered record. [MIL-26](#mil-26) (`specs/milestones/delivered.md:7407-7410`): the X61 record lists a lane as unbuilt and points to B484, but B484 describes that lane as built.

**Open work with no owner.** [MIL-34](#mil-34) (`specs/milestones/delivered.md:16670`): about ten closed records say a live run "is owed", and no item or ledger row carries it. [MIL-37](#mil-37) (`specs/milestones/m1.md:772-776`): two safety notes on the erase path exist only in B1533's prose. They disappear when that item is accepted.

**Delivery state inside normative rules.** [SUB-17](#sub-17) (`specs/substrates.md:1626`): one present-tense sentence disables the hosted KubeVirt lifecycle that the rest of the section describes. The parked item that tracks this gap is not named. [SEC-31](#sec-31) (`specs/security.md:1051-1054`) and [OCP-21](#ocp-21) (`specs/openshift-clusters.md:1278-1281`) state availability or a known safety gap inside a rule, not in the `Not yet met` form (C3). The patterns [OCP-P3](#ocp-p3), [ADD-P1](#add-p1) and [SEC-P1](#sec-p1) show the same thing in coverage tables. [HAR-14](#har-14) (`specs/state-reconciliation.md:868-871`) shows the reverse: `Not yet met` paragraphs that hold acceptance state or a declined option, not an unmet rule.

**Narrative an implementer must read past.** [MIL-46](#mil-46) (`specs/milestones/m2.md:1441-1442`) and [MIL-158](#mil-158) (`specs/milestones/m1.md:646-658`): open sections keep delivered narrative, cause hunts and test inventories. Some of it restates rules that `ceph-resources.md` owns, so each copy can drift.

The cause shows in the findings. Each slice adds text to an item section, a delivered record and often the spec. No step removes the text when the state changes: an item moves to awaiting acceptance, a later record closes a gap, or X444 accepts a set of items ([MIL-146](#mil-146)). The page rules say what a section holds, but most checks do not hold it. The docs check skips slice-less `in progress` items ([MIL-3](#mil-3)), nothing checks the Requires column, and nothing checks that an awaiting item names a gate. Many sections also open as a free record of the session, with no fixed shape for a delivery note, so narrative grows where the outcome and the exit evidence should be.

Two things are right and should stay. Ids are stable join keys across item rows, decisions, delivered records and Refs lines, so search by id works except where an id was reused. And the C3 form, one `Not yet met` paragraph ending at its item's link, is the right tool. The defects are places that skip it, not the form itself.

To fix the class, define "open item" once and keep items that await acceptance apart from work an agent can take. Cut each open section to its outcome, its exit evidence and its remaining work, and link to the delivered record for the rest. Move delivery state out of normative pages into C3 paragraphs or milestone rows, and extend the docs checks to the cases above. [Section 7](#7-the-plan) owns the steps.

### 6.2 The decision log

The decision log records each decision well when it is taken. It does not show later what still binds. When a later decision changes an earlier one, the earlier entry usually does not say so. Clauses that wait for the owner's review are not all on the review list, and normative pages cite decisions inside rule sentences without showing their state. An agent that follows a decision link can therefore read a rule that no longer holds.

The audit found 35 findings in this class: 16 Medium and 19 Low, none High. All 35 are single defects; none is a pattern of form. 23 are new, 7 are Low findings whose status nobody judged, 3 were already reported by audit 004 and are still present, 1 is tracked and 1 is settled. Four were found by more than one lane.

| Area | Medium | Low | Total |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| MIL | 11 | 10 | 21 |
| CEPH | 2 | 0 | 2 |
| SUB | 0 | 2 | 2 |
| MOS | 0 | 2 | 2 |
| HAR | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| API, REC, CTX, SEC, SVC, ADD | 2 | 4 | 6 |

The measured log behind these findings is in [section 2.11](#211-delivery-pages): 281 entries, 51% of `backlog.md`, 33 `session-pending` entries with about 263 clauses, and only 6 of 24 changed entries that name the decision that changed them.

The findings that matter most:

- **The review list is incomplete.** [MIL-12](#mil-12): the Open session clauses list says it "names each decision holding such a clause" (`specs/milestones/backlog.md:4184-4187`). It lists only the 33 `session-pending` entries. About 24 entries with the token `owner` also hold clauses pending review, some on the disk-erase path. [MIL-31](#mil-31) and [MIL-40](#mil-40) show pending clauses that live only in a delivered record or an item (`specs/milestones/m1.md:2944-2945`) and in no decision at all.
- **Changed entries still read as current.** [MIL-14](#mil-14): the earlier entry rarely names the later one, for example D143 does not mention D157 (`specs/milestones/backlog.md:5054`). [MIL-19](#mil-19) and [MIL-101](#mil-101) give clause-level cases: a power refusal during destroy, a node ceiling, a field name and a TLS transport that later decisions replaced. [MIL-15](#mil-15): D152 still says it "is a proposal and authorizes nothing" (`specs/milestones/backlog.md:4984`), although D154 accepted it.
- **A credential rule in the log contradicts the spec.** [MIL-18](#mil-18) and [SUB-40](#sub-40): D202 still says a lent KubeVirt token "is bound to no object" and that "the lifetime bound is its only revocation" (`specs/milestones/backlog.md:6688-6689`). D245 (6) and the substrates page require a marked Secret and a revoke. An agent can drop the revoke step.
- **The list keeps dead clauses.** [MIL-13](#mil-13): D159 (16), D241 and part of D203 (4) stay listed with no note that later decisions overrode them (`specs/milestones/backlog.md:4204-4205`). [MIL-87](#mil-87): no `accepted-by` token is newer than 2026-10-30, so the queue does not drain.
- **Specs keep an old decision state.** [CEPH-7](#ceph-7): the profile catalog still says "Until OD21 is answered" (`specs/ceph-coverage.md:214-221`) after D160 answered it. [CEPH-133](#ceph-133) states a per-client revocation that D160 moved to B491 (`specs/ceph-resources.md:659-660`). [ADD-6](#add-6) parks a forwarding mechanism that D246 adopted.
- **Decision ids sit inside rule sentences.** [HAR-4](#har-4) and [CTX-56](#ctx-56): `specs/controller.md:112-113` cites superseded D20 for a rule. [MIL-95](#mil-95) and [SUB-35](#sub-35): some rules carry "pending the owner's Q60 under D173" (`specs/project.md:113`), while others that rest on pending decisions, such as D240, carry no mark. [SEC-38](#sec-38) cites D160 for a rule that D160 does not hold.
- **The scope rule and the log disagree.** [MIL-4](#mil-4): `specs/milestones.md:41-42` says no decision "authorizes implementation or effect", but the log says a decision "authorizes" 77 times.

The cause is visible in the findings. The log is append-only: a new decision states its change in its own text, and nothing writes back to the entry it changes, to the review list or to the spec sentences that cite it. The status token describes the whole entry and has no form for a partial change ([MIL-14](#mil-14), [MIL-87](#mil-87)), and the decision test checks only that each `session-pending` entry is listed ([MIL-12](#mil-12)). Specs cite decisions as the basis of a rule ([HAR-35](#har-35), [MIL-62](#mil-62)), so every stale entry is one link away from a rule sentence.

Two things are right and should stay. The specs, not the log, mostly state the rules: one lane sampled 25 uncited decisions and found none with a product rule the specs lack. And D203 shows the form that works: it notes inside its own text that D278 overturned part of its clause (4).

The fix is one rule set for the log, not 35 local edits. A change to a decision writes a short pointer into the entry it changes, and the review list follows the state of each clause, not the token of the entry. Rule sentences in the specs carry no decision ids, and review state lives only in the log. A test can hold all three. [Section 7](#7-the-plan) gives the details.

## 7. The plan

This section is a proposal. It authorizes nothing: under the
[scope rules](../../specs/milestones.md#scope-rules) work starts only when the
owner asks for it and items are recorded. Three planners drew up independent
plans from different angles, three judges scored them, the orchestrator wrote
this one from their work, and a critic then attacked it
([section 8.6](#86-the-plan-stage)).

### 7.1 What the plan has to solve

The audit's findings come down to six causes. The plan is ordered by what each
one costs when a reader, human or agent, gets it wrong.

1. **Some rules are unsafe or contradict each other on paths that matter.**
   33 findings are High. In at least six of them the code already
   follows the wrong rule, and three of those are on secret or destructive
   paths: [SEC-2](#sec-2), [API-3](#api-3) and [SEC-1](#sec-1).
2. **Code and text change apart.** Behavior exists in the code that no page
   states (76 findings, four of them High), and text describes
   mechanics the code does not follow (82). An agent that rebuilds
   such code from the spec drops the unstated rule.
3. **A slice edits the pages it touches, and the copies elsewhere stay.** Of
   752 facts that two or more pages state, 134 have drifted
   ([section 2.7](#27-repetition)). Names of removed commands survive inside
   remedies ([CTX-1](#ctx-1), [CLI-2](#cli-2)).
4. **Tables are trusted more than they are checked.** 34 of 71 inventories
   have no test; the tests that exist each leave a column unchecked; and at
   least 11 tests that hold a spec table are missing from the list that the
   fast check tier runs
   ([section 2.8](#28-inventories-and-the-tests-that-hold-them)).
5. **The form of the text hides rules.** Half of the sampled sentences carry
   more than one rule, one in seven is above 40 words, and nine effect rules
   in ten name no check ([sections 2.5](#25-sentence-form) and
   [2.9](#29-effect-rules-proof-failure-and-test)). The index sends an agent
   to a whole page for most questions
   ([section 2.2](#22-how-an-agent-reaches-a-rule)).
6. **The corpus grows faster than it is consolidated**: about 164 KB of
   normative text a week, with 24 budget exceptions unchanged for four weeks,
   259 items awaiting acceptance and 33 decisions awaiting review
   ([sections 2.1](#21-size-and-growth), [2.4](#24-units-of-loading-sections-and-budgets)
   and [2.11](#211-delivery-pages)).

The order follows from that. Causes 1 and 2 change what the product does, so
they come first. Cause 4 comes beside them, because every later change of
text relies on those checks. Cause 3 follows, page by page. Cause 5 moves the
most text and changes no behavior, so it comes last and only after a measured
pilot. Cause 6 is mostly work that only the owner can do, acceptance and the
review of decisions; the plan only stops it from creating new defects.

### 7.2 Rules for every slice

These guard rails apply to all the work below. They exist because the work
changes text that decides behavior, and because agents will do it.

- **One disposition per finding**, named in the slice brief and in the commit
  body:
  - *Code follows text.* The spec is right, or is corrected. Spec, code, test
    and examples change in one commit, and the new test fails on the parent
    commit first.
  - *Text follows code.* The code is right and the page is silent or wrong.
    Each new sentence names the code symbol and the test that holds it. When
    no test exists, the slice adds one, and its commit is then not text-only.
    On a privilege, secret or destructive path a reviewer under the
    [security-safety](../../.agents/skills/security-safety/SKILL.md) skill
    first confirms that the code is right: describing unsafe code turns it
    into a rule.
  - *The owner decides.* The slice adds only a `Not yet met` paragraph and an
    item until the owner chooses.
- **The safer side wins by default** when text and code disagree on a safety
  path, unless an owner decision already chose the other side
  ([decision 3](#711-decisions-only-the-owner-can-take)). The owner sees the
  list before each slice and can overrule any case.
- **Check the finding against the current main first.** The audit read
  `e88d0c6cb`. Main has moved since, and other sessions edit the same pages.
  A slice does not start on a page that another active slice is editing.
- **Content and form never share a commit.** An unsafe rule is fixed before
  anyone rewords it; otherwise the error survives in better prose.
- **A commit that moves text changes no word. A commit that rewrites text
  moves nothing.** A reviewer can then compare like with like.
- **A text-only commit proves that it lost nothing.** A small tool
  ([K5](#75-lane-k-checks)) compares the literals of the normative pages
  before and after the commit: codes, flags, paths, numbers with units and
  test names. Every literal that leaves a page is named in the commit body
  with where it went: another page, or a link to the section that still
  states it. A refusal code may leave the corpus only when the code or the
  stop catalog changes in the same commit.
- **Fix the section that owns the fact, and replace each other statement of
  it with a link.** A slice never fixes a copy without fixing the owning
  section.
- **The reviewer is independent.** An Opus-class reviewer reads the cited code
  and the text before and after, not the implementer's summary. Before the
  first text-follows-code slice (C2), the review step and the K5 tool are
  tested once with a seeded rewrite that drops one condition; both must catch
  it.
- **Finding ids stay out of the specs.** The delivered record maps each
  finding to its item, as D252 set for the previous audit. This report is not
  edited.

### 7.3 Step 0: before the first slice

1. **One sitting of owner decisions**
   ([section 7.11](#711-decisions-only-the-owner-can-take)). Four answers are
   needed before anything starts: 1, 2, 3 and 5. Each of the others is needed
   before the slice that depends on it.
2. **Items**, in one docs commit that the owner's answers to decisions 1 and 2
   authorize: one item per High finding and one per workstream, each listing
   the finding ids it resolves and naming its milestone, out of sequence as
   D252 did for audit 004. One item per defect would add about 1,260 rows to
   pages that 365 open items already fill.
3. **Re-check the High findings on the current main**: one Sonnet run per
   finding, an Opus run for those on a privilege, secret or destructive path.
   What a later commit already changed is dropped or re-scoped.

### 7.4 Lane C: content

Lane C changes what the text says. It runs as one sequence, one active slice
at a time.

**C1. Rules that the code follows wrongly** (3 slices, safety class; code
follows text).

| Finding | The change | The test that fails first |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [SEC-2](#sec-2): `secret delete` is not refused under an effect-material hold, so delete then generate replaces the only readable copy | `specs/secrets.md` "Effect material under a live binding" lists delete among the refused writers; `Service.Delete` checks the hold | `TestDeleteRefusesALiveEffectMaterialBinding` |
| [API-3](#api-3): a plain `http://` BMC counts as verified for physical erase | One definition of a verified BMC in `specs/secrets.md`: an `https://` address whose `tls.verification` is absent, `full` or `certificate`. Every consumer links it. The slice also reads the other callers of the weak predicate (`BMCVerified` in `internal/substrate`), not erase alone; decision 6 settles what admission does with an `http://` address | `TestEraseRefusesAPlainHTTPBMC` |
| [SEC-1](#sec-1) and [CLI-1](#cli-1): elevated reveals do not check sudo's output log, and two rules name a sudo proof that no page defines | After decision 5: one section of `specs/secrets.md`, with its own anchor, defines the proof for input and for output logging; the reveal commands refuse when sudo's listing turns output logging on; `cli.md` links the section from both rules | `TestElevatedRevealRefusesSudoOutputLogging` |

Before each tighter refusal lands, the slice searches the examples, the
end-to-end fixtures and the input charts for inputs it would now refuse, and
the commit body says what an operator must change.

**C2. Safety rules that live only in code, or in a decision** (3 slices; text
follows code, with the security review of
[section 7.2](#72-rules-for-every-slice)). [API-4](#api-4): delegated sessions
refuse identity overrides and disable forwarding. [API-2](#api-2): the
ownership proof for removing a managed login. [CEPH-4](#ceph-4): the
CephClient attempt record and its refusal. [SEC-4](#sec-4): an authored OLM
add-on runs code with the privileges that code requests. [SEC-3](#sec-3): the
restated retry becomes a link to its owning section. [OCP-1](#ocp-1): the
rule for private downloads states the exception that the owner's decision
D269 already made, with its cost, in one place; the other pages link it.

**C3. Fields that nothing acts on, and paths that no page makes safe** (1
slice now; the behavior later). [API-1](#api-1), [SUB-1](#sub-1),
[SUB-2](#sub-2), [MOS-1](#mos-1), [MOS-2](#mos-2) and [SEC-51](#sec-51) each
need a choice by the owner (decisions 7 to 12). Until the choice, each gets a
`Not yet met` paragraph and an item, so that the page stops promising what
nothing does. This records the hazard; it does not remove it. Decision 7
comes before the slice, because its recommended answer removes a field
instead of describing it.

**C4. Contradictions on recovery and outcome paths** (about 6 slices).
[REC-1](#rec-1), [ADD-2](#add-2), [CLI-3](#cli-3), [CLI-4](#cli-4) and
[CTX-2](#ctx-2) change code or a contract beside the text: the six "no usable
outcome" stops become `unproved`; a failed read of an add-on object gets the
observe-again remedy; the stop catalog gains a column for the stops that
confine a removal failure, and a definition for every Recovery value; the
fresh-install remedies name the media deletion. Scripts read the `recovery`
value, so a row that changes class is a breaking change: a `!` commit whose
body names the impact and the remedy, with the `Contract:` line that
`scripts/check-commits` asks of a commit under a contract path.
[ARC-1](#arc-1), [ADD-1](#add-1), [REC-2](#rec-2), [OCP-2](#ocp-2),
[CEPH-3](#ceph-3) and [CEPH-129](#ceph-129) are text that follows the code or
the owning section. So are [CEPH-1](#ceph-1), [CEPH-2](#ceph-2),
[REC-74](#rec-74) and [ARC-37](#arc-37), but each of these four writes down
privilege, credential or erase behavior, so the security review applies to
them by name.

**C5. Names that no longer exist** (2 slices). [CTX-1](#ctx-1) and
[CLI-2](#cli-2), with the operator-facing constant that still says
`bootwright plan` and its fixtures. The checks of [K2](#75-lane-k-checks)
land first; these slices then empty their lists.

**C6a. Medium findings that can harm what Bootwright does not own** (about 3
slices, safety class). [CTX-23](#ctx-23): a resumed install counts another
tool's packages as its own, and uninstall removes them; it needs decision 13.
[CTX-26](#ctx-26), [SUB-21](#sub-21), [SUB-15](#sub-15), [MOS-21](#mos-21)
and [MOS-15](#mos-15) are of the same kind. They come before the pause point
of [section 7.6](#76-the-pause-point-and-the-gate) because their consequence,
not their rating, is the heaviest among the Medium findings.

**C6. The other Medium findings on safety, failure and missing rules** (about
20 slices, batched by owning page). 34 Medium findings concern a
proof, an authorization or a bound; 28 leave failure behavior
unstated; 40 are binding behavior that no page states;
41 are text and code that differ. Disclosure comes first:
[CLI-46](#cli-46), [CEPH-27](#ceph-27), [SVC-10](#svc-10),
[CEPH-55](#ceph-55) and [SEC-24](#sec-24). Rules that live only in a
milestone item, a delivered record or a knowledge page move into their owning
spec here, and a knowledge page that contradicts the spec on the same rule is
corrected in the same slice ([section 9.2](#92-the-corpus-proposals-that-were-not-taken-up)).
Each effect section a slice touches gains two closing lines, `Code:` and
`Held by:`, naming the package and the tests that a reviewer has read
([section 5.4](#54-tables-and-rules-that-no-check-holds)).

**C7. Rules that pages state differently** (about 16 slices, one per subject
of [section 2.7](#27-repetition), the subjects with the most drift first).
For each drifted fact the owning section is made right and the other
statements become links. 104 Medium findings name such pairs, and
87 more are a page that contradicts itself. A contradiction with no
clear owning section, or one where both sides are plausible designs, becomes
a question for the owner, not an edit.

### 7.5 Lane K: checks

Lane K adds checks. It changes no rule, so it runs beside lane C from the
first day. A check that reads the pages starts with a list of today's known
violations: it fails on any new one, and the list may only get shorter. Each
has a test of its own violations, in the style of `TestDocsHistoryViolations`,
carries the `TestDocs` name that the check list expects, and reads the
normative pages only: milestone pages and deferred designs keep the names
they recorded.

| # | Check | What it would have caught | Known violations today |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| K1 | `TestDocsChecksListIsComplete` is extended: every test that opens a page under `specs/`, whatever its name, is in `test/docs/testdata/docs-checks.txt` | at least 11 table-holding tests that the fast tier does not run | 0 after the slice |
| K5 | `scripts/check-commits` gains the literal comparison of [section 7.2](#72-rules-for-every-slice), for a commit that changes normative pages and nothing else. It is part of the commit check, not of the test list | a rewrite that drops a code, a bound, a flag or a test name | none |
| K2 | `TestDocsCommandLinesMatchTheCatalog` also reads the `bootwright ...` code spans of the normative pages, with their flags. A check beside `TestDiagnosticCodesMatchOutputSpec` holds every backticked code of a registered family to the registry. `TestDocsLinksNameAUniqueHeading`: no link names an anchor that several headings of its target page share | [CTX-1](#ctx-1), [CLI-2](#cli-2) and the command and code part of the stale-reference class; the 13 links to the shared anchor of `managed-os.md` | lists that only shrink |
| K3 | Each refusal-table test gains one case per Path condition of its rows, and the Ceph one exercises the placement policy ([CEPH-45](#ceph-45)). The stop-catalog test compares the new "Confines removal" column and requires a definition for every Recovery value. The 34 unheld inventories become a list that only shrinks | [CLI-3](#cli-3), [CLI-4](#cli-4); the six unheld inventories that had drifted | 34 |
| K4 | A per-page count of the availability phrases ("refused until", "is parked", "currently", "today") outside the `Not yet met` form, which may only fall. The normative sentences that cite a decision the owner has not reviewed are kept as a list. The existing decision test also requires the list "Open session clauses" to name an `owner` entry that holds a pending clause | growth of the 37 unmet rules stated outside the form; rules that rest on 16 unreviewed decisions; 24 entries missing from the list ([MIL-12](#mil-12)) | the page counts; 16; 24 |

Notes on what these checks cannot do:

- K1 and K5 come first, with the first slice of lane C. The fast tier,
  `make focus`, runs only the listed tests, so until K1 lands a spec-only
  slice reaches its last gate before the test that holds its table has run.
  The full gate at integration does run them.
- K2 does not ask that headings be unique: a page with several capabilities
  repeats "Selection", "Implementations" and "Refusal table" by design. It
  asks that no link depends on which of them comes first. It reads flags only
  inside a `bootwright` command, because the pages also name the flags of
  native tools.
- The list of unheld inventories in K3 cannot see a new inventory; only a
  reviewer can. It stops the known ones from being forgotten.
- The phrase count in K4 cannot tell an unmet rule from rule language such as
  "currently owns". Of 62 such statements that a lane classified, 37 are unmet
  rules; C6 removes those, and the count keeps the rest from growing.
- The list of citations in K4 is not a ban. A clause that a session took
  binds until the owner overturns it. The list shows the owner which rules
  rest on clauses nobody has reviewed.

Seven slices cover the lane.

### 7.6 The pause point and the gate

After C1 to C5, C6a and K1 to K5:

- every High finding is fixed, or recorded as a gap with an item and a
  question for the owner;
- the six Medium findings that can harm what Bootwright does not own are
  fixed;
- the commonest ways for these defects to return are checked;
- no page is half changed.

The program can pause here. The six findings of C3 are still live hazards
until their decisions are taken and built, and the other Medium findings
(C6, C7) remain.

Before anything larger starts:

1. **Keep the measuring stick in the repository.** A reference file beside
   the architecture skill holds the 12 dry-run tasks, the 30 routing
   questions and this report's baseline, so that the same measurement can be
   repeated.
2. **Sort the guesses.** [Section 5.1](#51-what-the-dry-runs-show) sorts the
   82 guesses of the dry runs: 31 are choices about the new feature that only
   the owner can make, and the corpus by its own convention does not hold
   them in advance. No work on form removes those. Another 23 are general
   rules for adding a field, a stop, a kind or a package; they belong in the
   two sections of `specs/architecture.md` that already list what such a
   change must touch, with a note on a capability's own page only where a dry
   run showed the gap.
3. **Run the measurement again** and compare it with
   [section 2.3](#23-what-a-coding-agent-loads-and-where-it-guesses).
4. **The owner decides** whether C7 and the form work go ahead, and after the
   pilot how far ([decisions 1 and 17](#711-decisions-only-the-owner-can-take)).

### 7.7 Lane F: form and routing

Everything in this lane changes no behavior.

**F0. A writing standard for new and touched text** (1 slice, beside K1; it
needs decision 4, not the gate). The corpus gains about 164 KB a week, so the
first aim is that new text stops adding to the backlog. A reference of the
architecture skill, `spec-form.md`, states the shape:

- a section opens with one sentence of scope: the actor, the trigger and what
  the section does not cover;
- one rule per sentence or list item, with its actor and its observable
  outcome (the refusal code, the state, the record);
- an enumeration is a list; a case analysis is a decision table; refusals are
  rows of code, condition and remedy;
- an effect section says what happens on failure, timeout, cancellation,
  crash and an unknown outcome;
- rationale is one `Why:` line or lives in the decision; a decision id
  appears only in a closing `Basis:` line, and an item id only in a
  `Not yet met` paragraph;
- an effect section closes with `Code:` and `Held by:`.

The passages that the lanes named as models
([section 4.1](#41-sentence-form)) are its examples. It is guidance for
writers and reviewers, not a gate.

**F1. Routing by section** (2 slices). Each page above the section budget
opens with a map of its sections, one line each saying what the section
decides, held by a test. The index's second table, "Sections of the largest
domains", moves into those maps, which frees the bytes for the five pages that
have no row; the index is 53 bytes under its budget today. The index then
routes to the page and the map routes to the section. Target: of the 30
routing questions, 20 land on the owning section within budget (about 6
today).

**F2. Budgets that measure what an agent loads** (1 slice). The size limit of
a `###` section counts its subsections too, and the text directly under a
`##` heading gets the limit of a smallest section. Both start from lists of
today's cases that only shrink (6 and 50).

**F3. One pilot** (2 to 3 slices), then the owner's review. One hard unit goes
through the whole treatment: `specs/contexts.md` "Storage, locking and
publication", 44 KB under one heading, the fourth largest exception. First a
commit that only splits it into named sections; then one rewrite commit per
section to the standard, each passing the literal comparison and two
independent readers who list the rules of the old and the new text and
compare them. The pilot reports its cost (agent runs, reviewer time), the
measurement of [section 7.6](#76-the-pause-point-and-the-gate) for questions
that land in it, and every difference the readers found.

**F4. The rest, page by page** (large; only after decision 17). The order is
by traffic and by distance from the standard:
`state-reconciliation.md`, `managed-os.md`, `substrates.md`, `ceph.md`,
`cli.md`, `openshift-clusters.md`, `controller.md`, `security.md`,
`infrastructure-services.md`, `architecture.md`, then the others. A page's
content findings are closed before its form slice. The 24 budget exceptions
fall with their pages, which is the work of parked item B965.

**F5. Words** (2 slices). Terms on safety paths first: the three senses of
"owner", "operator" for the person against the OLM operator, and "qualified"
([GOV-1](#gov-1)). The glossary's false "always" and "never" statements are
corrected. Other terms are defined when a fix needs them, as the corpus's
convention asks.

### 7.8 Lane D: delivery pages

These pages are the owner's working records, so the plan proposes little
here and automates less.

- **D1. Review debt.** The owner reviews the 16 pending decisions that
  normative rules cite, then the other pending decisions in batches
  ([decision 15](#711-decisions-only-the-owner-can-take)). K4 keeps the list
  of rules that rest on them.
- **D2. State that contradicts itself** (2 slices). Items in progress with no
  slice, Requires cells naming closed items, the Status table against the
  pages ([section 6](#6-delivery-pages)). The 37 Medium findings
  on delivery state are corrected in the same slices. Where a later decision
  changed an earlier one, the earlier entry gains one appended line that
  names it, if the owner allows appends to old entries (decision 15); nothing
  else in an old entry changes.
- **D3. The shape of a new delivered record**
  ([decision 16](#711-decisions-only-the-owner-can-take)). A record keeps
  what was delivered, its evidence, the finding-to-item map and its limits,
  and links the spec for the rule.
- **D4. Acceptance.** An item whose exit evidence names only in-tree gates
  completes when they pass
  ([completion and verification](../../specs/milestones.md#completion-and-verification)).
  The items of C2, lane K and lane F are written that way, so they add
  nothing to the 259 items that already await acceptance. The items of C3
  stay open until their behavior lands.

A size is S for one slice, M for two to five, L for more. At most two slices
are active: one of lane C, and one of lane K or, later, lane F.

| K1, K5 | The check list is complete; the literal comparison | M | | |

| K2 | Names must exist; links name one heading | M | | |

| K3, K4 | Held tables; availability and review lists | M | | |
| C6a | Medium findings that can harm what Bootwright does not own | M, safety class | decision 13 | |
| | **Pause point** | | | **27 fixed, 6 recorded** |
| C3, built | The behavior the owner chose for the six recorded gaps | M to L, safety class | decisions 7 to 12 | 6 fixed |
| C6 | The other Medium safety, failure, missing-rule and mismatch findings | L | | |

What it costs the owner, up to the pause point: about 28 slices. Eleven or so
change product behavior (C1, part of C4, C6a) and are safety class, so each
carries an independent review and a race run. The others are text and checks,
and their items complete on in-tree gates. The owner's own part is the
sitting of decisions, a reading of the slices that change behavior, and the
review of the 16 pending decisions. The audit did not measure how long that
takes; the first three slices will show it.
